name: Pedro Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a grader at an open-pit nickel mine. The grader is the long machine with a blade under the middle, and my crew keeps the haul roads smooth and drained so the big trucks don't wreck their tyres. I'm leading hand for the road crew, three graders and two water carts. Every morning I drive the whole road network with the shift boss, note the potholes and soft spots, and plan the day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a craft. A good grader operator can take a road from a mess to a table in one pass, and the truck drivers thank you for it. What wears me out is worry about the nickel price, because the mine cut a whole shift last year when it dropped. My girlfriend Ana works at the medical clinic front desk, and I send money to my mum every month, so we've got barely three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Then my real problem is still the nickel price, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's get back to work. At work I'd say the same as always, keep the roads right and the trucks moving. I'd maybe say a word at church about being grateful for steady work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried, because the shift cut last year had nothing to do with AI. If nickel drops again, the road crew goes from three graders to two, and I'm leading hand but not untouchable. That's the thing that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and put another hundred a fortnight into savings, even if it hurts. I'd ask about grading farm roads on weekends for the farmers around town, cash work. I'd use the AI on my phone now and then to write up the quotes, like Ana showed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not new worried. The same old worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the road crew dropped to two graders, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope to keep my seat, but if not, I'd ask to go onto the water carts. Lower pay, but it's work. I'd never sit at home waiting for a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the money you send your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That stays. My dad passed three years ago and my sisters are still at school. I'd cut my own things before hers.

say: I'd say **get back** to work and keep the roads right.
At **church** I'd say a word of thanks for steady work.
think: Last year's **shift cut** came from the nickel price, not AI.
If nickel drops again, the crew loses a **grader**, and I'm not untouchable.
do: Grade **farm roads** on weekends for cash.
Use the phone **AI** now and then for quotes.
feel: **Worried**, with the same old worry rather than a new one.
S0.quote: If nickel drops again, the road crew goes from three graders to two, and I'm leading hand but not untouchable.
fieldNote: His fear comes from the **nickel price**, which already cost a shift.
He supports his **mum and sisters** and protects that money first.
He'd take **lower pay** rather than be idle.

steps.text: Put an extra hundred dollars a fortnight into savings
Grade farm roads on weekends for local farmers
Keep leading the road crew on the same shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots spreading slowly. I've seen videos of driverless graders, but our roads change every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change comes, and the people who work hard will find a place. At work I'd tell the young ones to learn the GPS blade control, because that's coming either way. I wouldn't moan about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the road crew is one of the later jobs to go, but the planning part goes now. The shift boss and I plan the roads every morning, and a computer could do that from the truck sensors. Then it's me just following a plan, and that's easier to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the GPS blade system properly, once the other mines have shown it works. I'd use the AI tools more, maybe to read the road reports. And I'd keep saving, because Ana's job at the clinic desk is exactly the answering-customers kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicked, but uneasy for both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Ana's job. What would happen there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clinic already talks about an online booking system. If that comes in, they need one receptionist instead of two. Ana's the newer one, so she'd likely go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd live on my pay, and I'd send less to Mum, which I'd hate. Ana would look for work at the school. We'd get through it.

say: Change comes, and people who **work hard** find a place.
Young operators should learn **GPS blade control**.
think: The road crew goes **later**, but the planning part goes now.
Once a computer plans the roads, I'm just **following a plan**.
do: Learn the **GPS blade** system once other mines prove it.
Use **AI tools** to read road reports.
Keep **saving**, because Ana's clinic job is at risk.
feel: **Uneasy** for both of them, but not panicked.
S1.quote: My partner Ana's job at the clinic desk is exactly the answering-customers kind.
fieldNote: He spots that **planning** is the first part of his job to go.
**Ana's receptionist** job is the household's real risk.
He waits for **proof** before learning the new system.

steps.text: Learn the GPS blade control system once proven elsewhere
Use AI tools to read the daily road reports
Save more in case Ana's clinic job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Ana's job would be gone almost straight away, wouldn't it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's in God's hands, but we should help each other through it. At work I'd say the company should train its own people before it buys robots. I'd talk to the pastor about how the church could help families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Ana's job goes in 2028, the planning part of mine goes then too, and the grader drives itself by 2031. That leaves me three years and a family to help. I'd be frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a diesel fitter apprenticeship at the mine straight away, because someone has to fix the machines. We'd put off getting married until we know what's happening. And I'd lean on the church and Ana's family if money ran out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like a road washing out under the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said before you'd never sit waiting for a cheque. Would you take government help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for training, not for sitting at home. A loan for a trade, yes. A handout, no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm still sending money, just less for a while. And I'd tell my sisters to study something that needs people, like nursing. She'd pray for us, which helps.

say: It's in **God's hands**, but we should help each other.
The company should **train its people** before buying robots.
think: Ana's job and my **planning** go in 2028, then the grader drives itself by 2031.
That leaves me **three years** and a family to help.
do: Start a **diesel fitter** apprenticeship straight away.
Put off the **wedding** until things are clearer.
Lean on **church and family** if money runs out.
feel: **Alarmed**, like a road washing out under the truck.
S2.quote: Only for training, not for sitting at home. A loan for a trade, yes. A handout, no.
fieldNote: He accepts state help **only for training**, never as a handout.
The household faces **two losses**: Ana's in 2028, his by 2031.
He leans on **faith and family** for support.

steps.text: Start a diesel fitter apprenticeship at the mine straight away
Put off the wedding with Ana until things are clearer
Ask the church and Ana's family for help if money runs out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to get a trade, if I start soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given time, so let's use it well. At work I'd push the company to run apprenticeships for operators. I'd keep it positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'm okay if I start the fitter apprenticeship next year. It takes four years, and I'd be done before 2031. The hard part is the apprentice wage while I'm still sending money home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard for a year to cover the pay drop. Then I'd start the apprenticeship. Ana would retrain too, maybe as a teacher's aide at the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but it feels like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How big is the pay drop for an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a third, for the first two years. That's the money for Mum and some. We'd need about five thousand put away first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then, for study, like checking a wiring diagram. Not for everything. I want to learn it properly, with my hands.

say: We've been **given time**, so let's use it well.
The company should run **apprenticeships** for its operators.
think: I'm **okay** if I start the fitter apprenticeship next year.
The hard part is the **apprentice wage** while sending money home.
do: **Save** about five thousand dollars in a year.
Back Ana's move to be a **teacher's aide**.
feel: **Nervous**, but it feels like a plan.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to get a trade, if I start soon.
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **four-year apprenticeship** plan.
The **pay drop** threatens the money he sends his mum.

steps.text: Save about five thousand dollars over the next year
Start a diesel fitter apprenticeship at the mine
Help Ana train as a teacher's aide at the school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, then robots around 2039. That's a long road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so nobody should be caught out. At work I'd keep pushing for apprenticeships. At church I'd say families should plan ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I can keep grading for a good few years. The nickel price would still worry me more. But I'd have time to build something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep grading at the mine. With my uncle, I'd buy an old grader on finance and do farm and council roads on weekends. Later, maybe it becomes a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. Still a bit worried about nickel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a grader on three weeks of savings sounds risky. Why do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle would put in the deposit, and I'd pay him back from the weekend jobs. Family helps family. It's a risk, but it's ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Ana marry sooner with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, next year, like we planned. With ten years I'm not scared to start a family. With two years I would be.

say: There's time, so **nobody** should be caught out.
Families should **plan ahead**, and I'd keep pushing for apprenticeships.
think: I can keep **grading** for a good few years.
The **nickel price** would still worry me more than robots.
do: Buy an old **grader** on finance with his uncle.
S4.quote: With ten years I'm not scared to start a family. With two years I would be.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him plan a **family business** with his uncle.
**Nickel prices** remain his main worry over robots.
Longer warning means he'll **marry** on schedule.

steps.text: Keep grading haul roads at the nickel mine
Buy an old grader on finance with his uncle
Marry Ana next year as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Ana's job goes almost at once, my planning goes too, and the grader drives itself three years later, all while I'm helping Mum. What would help is the company paying for apprenticeships for its own operators, and loans for a trade that you pay back once you're working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the nickel price. People talk about robots like they're the only thing that can take your job. Out here, a bad year on the metal market does it faster.

headlineQuote: Out here, a bad year on the metal market takes your job faster than any robot.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old** grader operator and road crew leading hand at an open-pit nickel mine.
He sends money to his **widowed mum**, lives with Ana, a clinic receptionist, and has three weeks saved.
He is **traditional**, takes training help but refuses handouts, and leans on church and family.
He sees **Ana's job** and the planning side of his own as the first to go.
With **five or ten years** he plans a fitter trade or a grading business with his uncle.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028**, with Ana's job gone at once and his three years later.
whatWouldHelp: **Training loans** paid back once you're working again.
